findings.before: adjust wrongly; block; disguise (die Stimme)
findings.after: adjust, move (a seat, a setting), also by mistake; block (a path); disguise (one's voice); sich verstellen: pretend
findings.why: verstellen is neutral 'adjust/move out of its position' far more often than 'adjust wrongly': den Sitz verstellen, höhenverstellbar, verstellbar = adjustable. 'adjust wrongly' teaches a false negative meaning; the very common reflexive 'sich verstellen' (pretend, put on an act) is missing.

findings.before: to adjust wrongly; to disguise
findings.after: to move out of place (a seat, a setting); to block (a path)
findings.why: Follows the corrected meaning; 'disguise' alone is weak as a clue since it normally needs 'die Stimme' or sich.

findings.before: Who has changed my seat setting?
findings.after: Who has moved my seat?
findings.why: More natural English for 'Wer hat meinen Sitz verstellt?' (car seat adjusted by someone else).

findings.before: to draw up (a document, a list)
findings.after: to create (a document, a website, a file)
findings.why: 'draw up (a list)' is also a sense of aufstellen in this same family (en of aufstellen: 'draw up (a list)'; eine Liste aufstellen); a learner can rightly answer aufstellen. erstellen's distinctive sense is creating a document/file/website.

findings.before: to surround (the police, a house)
findings.after: to surround (as police do with a house)
findings.why: '(the police, a house)' reads as if the police were the ones surrounded.

findings.before: Der Bote stellt das Paket morgen zu.
findings.after: Das Paket wird morgen zugestellt.
findings.why: zustellen is almost always used in the passive or by the Post as subject; 'Der Bote stellt ... zu' sounds constructed.

findings.before: The courier will deliver the parcel tomorrow.
findings.after: The parcel will be delivered tomorrow.
findings.why: Matches the passive example.

findings.before: I am leaving the bike in the courtyard.
findings.after: I park my bike in the courtyard.
findings.why: The clue says 'to park (a bike)'; the translation should show that sense, and the German present here is habitual.

findings.before: position (posture, rank); stance
findings.after: position (posture, rank); stance; Stellung nehmen (zu): comment on, take a stand
findings.why: The most frequent use of Stellung for a learner is the fixed phrase Stellung nehmen zu; it is also the base of die Stellungnahme.

findings.before: official statement (taking a position)
findings.after: statement, comment (giving your position on something)
findings.why: A Stellungnahme need not be official: a student writes eine Stellungnahme in Goethe B2 Schreiben, a person gives one.

findings.before: the employment (a post you hold)
findings.after: the employment (being employed by someone)
findings.why: 'a post you hold' also fits die Stelle (clue: 'the job'); remove the overlap.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: Common at trade fairs and on documents (Aussteller of a passport/invoice); B2 is a fairer fit.

findings.after: verstellbar, einstellbar, herstellbar, darstellbar, feststellbar, zustellbar, der Besteller, der Aufsteller
findings.why: The B2 board offers the ending bar with ver/ein/her/dar/fest/zu; verstellbar (adjustable) is a very common word, and the others are real. B1 board be+er gives Besteller, auf+er Aufsteller (display stand). None of these should ever be called wrong.

findings.before: fill (a roll); take (a course); prove (with evidence)
findings.after: take (a course); prove, document (with evidence); put a topping on (a roll); occupy (a seat, a place)
findings.why: 'fill' is wrong for a Brötchen: belegen = put cheese/ham ON it. 'occupy' (belegt = taken, a seat; Platz eins belegen) is missing.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: einen Kurs belegen, belegtes Brötchen, besetzt/belegt are everyday words; C1 is too high.

findings.before: interpret (a text, a law); lay out (goods)
findings.after: interpret (a text, a law); lay out (goods); pay for someone for now (Geld auslegen); cover (a floor)
findings.why: 'Kannst du mir das Geld auslegen?' is the most frequent everyday use and is missing.

findings.before: Board A2: hinlegen, überlegen, auflegen, einlegen, weglegen, die_Anlage
findings.after: (keep, or tag the board B1)
findings.why: Four of six words are tagged B1 and only hinlegen is A2; the A2 board is effectively a B1 board.

findings.before: Board B1: überlegen, die_Überlegung, ablegen, anlegen, die_Anlage, festlegen, vorlegen, die_Vorlage, verlegen, zurücklegen
findings.after: (swap some B2 forms for B1 ones, or tag the board B2)
findings.why: Seven of ten forms are tagged B2 (Überlegung, ablegen, anlegen, festlegen, vorlegen, Vorlage, verlegen).

findings.before: entlegen, erlegen, unterlegen
findings.after: add: die Zulage, die Auslage, widerlegbar, belegbar, auslegbar, die Widerlegung, die Darlegung, die Belegung, die Zerlegung, die Beilegung, die Rücklage/Zurücklage
findings.why: Real words reachable with the B2 tiles (zu/aus + e, wider/be/aus + bar, + ung); Zulage (bonus, allowance) and Auslage (shop window display; expenses) are common.

findings.before: Für das Gespräch brauchen wir einen Übersetzer.
findings.after: Für den Vertrag brauchen wir einen Übersetzer.
findings.why: For a spoken conversation German uses der Dolmetscher (interpreter); Übersetzer translates written text. The example teaches the learner the wrong word for interpreting, a distinction German teachers and Goethe materials insist on.

findings.before: We need a translator for the meeting.
findings.after: We need a translator for the contract.
findings.why: Follows the corrected example.

findings.before: adv
findings.after: adj
findings.why: grundsätzlich is an adjective (eine grundsätzliche Frage) also used as an adverb.

findings.before: in principle; fundamentally
findings.after: in principle; as a rule, on principle (Ich esse grundsätzlich kein Fleisch); fundamental
findings.why: German grundsätzlich often means 'always, without exception, on principle', almost the opposite of English 'in principle (but...)'. The learner should see both.

findings.before: stop for a moment, cut out (an engine); abandon (an animal)
findings.after: cut out, stop (an engine, the heart); abandon (an animal); expose (to: jemanden etwas aussetzen); suspend; etwas auszusetzen haben: find fault
findings.why: 'expose to' and 'etwas auszusetzen haben' are the commonest uses after B1 and are missing.

findings.before: zersetzen, entsetzen, widersetzen
findings.after: add: der Durchsatz, der Versatz, der Aussatz, der Besatz, die Besetzung, die Ersetzung
findings.why: Real words reachable with the B2/B1 tiles (durch/ver/aus/be + stem; be/er + ung). They should never be called wrong.

findings.before: vernehmen, ausnehmen, durchnehmen
findings.after: add: die Hinnahme, die Vornahme, die Entnahme, die Mitnahme, die Zurücknahme, der Aufnehmer, der Einnehmer
findings.why: Real nouns reachable with the B1/B2 tiles (hin/vor/ent/mit + e; zurück + e on B1; auf/ein + er). Entnahme and Mitnahme are frequent.

findings.before: I will take you along.
findings.after: I'll give you a lift. / I'll take you with me.
findings.why: 'Ich nehme dich mit' most often means giving someone a lift; 'take you along' is stiff.

findings.before: Board B1: ... die_Annahme, die_Aufnahme, die_Übernahme ...
findings.after: (fine, optional: tag B1/B2)
findings.why: Three of ten forms on the B1 board are tagged B2; acceptable but worth a look.

findings.before: hat/ist undefined
findings.after: hat/ist gezogen
findings.why: Data bug: the Partizip II renders as 'undefined'. ziehen: hat gezogen (pull), ist gezogen (move house).

findings.before: to hand over (keys); to be sick (sich)
findings.after: to hand over formally (a flat, keys to a tenant); to vomit (sich)
findings.why: 'Den Schlüssel abgeben' is extremely common and abgeben's en lists 'hand over', so 'hand over (keys)' invites abgeben. 'to be sick' means 'ill' to American readers; sich übergeben is only vomit.

findings.before: hand over; sich übergeben: be sick
findings.after: hand over (formally); sich übergeben: vomit
findings.why: 'be sick' is ambiguous (ill vs. vomit); a learner may say 'Ich habe mich übergeben' meaning 'I was ill'.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: ergeben is very frequent (wordfreq 4.57): 'Das ergibt Sinn', 'Die Umfrage hat ergeben, dass ...', 'Daraus ergibt sich'. C1 understates it.

findings.before: sich, never splits
findings.after: never splits (also sich)
findings.why: The non-reflexive ergeben (yield, show, amount to: 'Drei mal drei ergibt neun') is at least as common as sich ergeben; marking it as a sich-verb teaches that 'Die Studie ergab ...' is wrong.

findings.before: The essay has to be handed in on Friday.
findings.after: The deadline for the term paper is Friday.
findings.why: German says the handing-in is on Friday (a deadline), and a Hausarbeit is a university term paper rather than a school essay.

findings.before: Wir kommen vom Weg ab.
findings.after: Wir sind vom Thema abgekommen.
findings.why: The present tense as a live report sounds odd; abkommen is almost always said in the Perfekt after the fact. The topic sense is also the one an adult uses most.

findings.before: We are straying from the path.
findings.after: We've got off the topic.
findings.why: Matches the proposed example.

findings.before: to meet halfway; to come towards
findings.after: to meet (someone) halfway; to come towards (someone, on the road)
findings.why: zukommen (same B2 board) has en 'come towards' and clue 'to come up to (someone)'; the bare 'to come towards' fits both. The 'meet halfway' part keeps it solvable, but the overlap invites zukommen.

findings.before: to come up to (someone); to lie ahead
findings.after: to walk up to (auf jemanden); to lie ahead (auf uns)
findings.why: Separates it more clearly from entgegenkommen 'come towards', and the auf hint shows the construction.

findings.before: Mit Englisch kommt man hier gut durch.
findings.after: Hier ist so viel los, man kommt kaum durch.
findings.why: The example shows 'get by', which the clue does not mention and which is auskommen's clue ('to get by (on money)'). The example should show the clue's sense (get through). Alternatively add 'get by' to the clue.

findings.before: You can get by here with English.
findings.after: It's so busy here, you can hardly get through.
findings.why: Matches the proposed example.

findings.before: leave, go away; go out
findings.after: leave, go away; (colloquial) go out (in the evening)
findings.why: Correct, but ausgehen on the same A2 board has the clue 'to go out (in the evening)'. A learner who reads this en will answer weggehen for it. Mark the sense as colloquial so the learner knows ausgehen is the standard answer.

findings.before: to wind up (a clock); to rear (a child)
findings.after: to wind up (a clock); to raise (a child, an animal: feed and care for); to tease (jemanden)
findings.why: erziehen is on the same B1 board with en 'bring up, educate'. 'to rear (a child)' can be answered with erziehen. The clue should name the physical raising, and the common 'tease' sense is missing.

findings.before: Board B1
findings.after: Board B2 only
findings.why: It is a B2 form, and on the B1 board it sits beside erziehen with an overlapping sense ('bring up a child'), so it is the most ambiguous pair on that board.

findings.before: er = to a result: pull a child up to adulthood.
findings.after: er = to a result: shape a child into a person with values and manners. (aufziehen = feed and raise.)
findings.why: It uses word for word the same picture as aufziehen ('pull a child up to adulthood'), which blurs the two verbs.

findings.before: She is bringing her children up bilingual.
findings.after: She is bringing her children up bilingually.
findings.why: The adverbial form is the standard English here.

findings.before: Ich ziehe Tee vor.
findings.after: Ich ziehe Tee dem Kaffee vor.
findings.why: Without a context or the dative comparison, the bare sentence sounds stiff. Also, 'Ich trinke lieber Tee' is what people say. The dative pattern (A dem B vorziehen) is the thing to learn.

findings.before: I prefer tea.
findings.after: I prefer tea to coffee.
findings.why: Matches the proposed example.

findings.before: draw (curtains) closed
findings.after: draw (curtains) closed; sich etwas zuziehen: catch, incur (a cold, an injury)
findings.why: 'sich eine Erkältung/Verletzung zuziehen' is a very frequent use, and a B2 learner will meet it in news and reports.

findings.before: I am writing about your advertisement.
findings.after: I am writing with reference to your advertisement.
findings.why: Keeps the 'refer to' meaning visible, and it is the standard English letter formula that matches the German one.

findings.before: Ich komme morgen beziehungsweise übermorgen.
findings.after: Die Karten kosten 10 bzw. 15 Euro für Kinder bzw. Erwachsene.
findings.why: As written, the sentence reads as 'tomorrow or the day after' and does not show 'or rather' (a correction normally needs a comma and context). The 'respectively' use with bzw. is by far the most common one in written German.

findings.before: I'm coming tomorrow, or rather the day after.
findings.after: Tickets cost 10 and 15 euros for children and adults respectively.
findings.why: Matches the proposed example.

findings.before: the move (to a new home)
findings.after: the move (from one home to another)
findings.why: der Einzug's clue also says '(to a new home)'. Wording Umzug as from-one-to-another keeps the two clearly apart.

findings.before: to be cut, to no longer apply (a rule)
findings.after: to be dropped, to disappear (jobs, a reason; everyday word)
findings.why: 'to no longer apply' is exactly what entfallen means (on forms: 'entfällt' = not applicable), and entfallen is on the same B2 board with the ent tile. A learner can reasonably build entfallen for this clue.

findings.before: to fall over (a person)
findings.after: to fall down, to trip and fall (a person)
findings.why: umfallen's clue is also 'to fall over', and the um tile sits on the same A2 board. 'Er ist umgefallen' works for a person too (fainted, toppled), so 'fall over' does not single out hinfallen.

findings.before: The child fell over in the street.
findings.after: The child fell down in the street.
findings.why: Keeps 'fall over' for umfallen and 'fall down' for hinfallen consistently.

findings.before: T
findings.after: M
findings.why: Its source here is zufallen = 'shut by itself (a door)'. Nothing in that gives 'coincidence'. The link (something that falls to you, comes your way) is a figurative step, so T is wrong.

findings.before: A2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: durchfallen (in einer Prüfung) is a B1 word in the Goethe word lists, not A2.

findings.before: Der Verfall des alten Hauses ist traurig.
findings.after: Die Stadt will den Verfall der Altstadt stoppen.
findings.why: The original is grammatical but stiff. A native would say 'Es ist traurig, wie das Haus verfällt'. 'Verfall stoppen/aufhalten' is the typical collocation. exEn: 'The town wants to stop the decay of the old town.'

findings.before: missfallen; befallen; herfallen; widerfallen
findings.after: add: anfällig (susceptible), überfällig (overdue), beifällig (approving), der Wegfall (removal, abolition), der Entfall (Austrian/administrative: omission)
findings.why: B2 tiles an/über/bei + -ig and weg/ent + stem build these real words (anfällig, überfällig and Wegfall are common B2 words). If the game rejects unlisted combinations, it would tell him common words are wrong.

findings.before: missfallen; befallen; herfallen; widerfallen
findings.after: add: gefällig (obliging; pleasing), ausfällig (abusive: ausfällig werden), abfällig (disparaging), auffällig (in the family, but not on this board)
findings.why: B1 tiles ge/aus/ab/auf + -ig build real adjectives that are not targets on this board.

findings.before: long-lasting; keeps (food)
findings.after: keeps (food, until a date); durable
findings.why: nachhaltig is on the same B2 board with the clue 'sustainable; lasting'. 'long-lasting' and 'lasting' point to both words ('eine nachhaltige Wirkung' = a long-lasting effect).

findings.before: sustainable; lasting
findings.after: sustainable (good for the environment); lasting (an effect)
findings.why: Separates it from haltbar on the same board. The disambiguator ties 'lasting' to an effect, not to food or material.

findings.before: Der Inhalt des Buches ist spannend.
findings.after: Fassen Sie den Inhalt des Textes kurz zusammen.
findings.why: A native says 'Das Buch ist spannend'. 'Der Inhalt ist spannend' sounds off. 'den Inhalt zusammenfassen' is the core collocation and appears in Goethe tasks. exEn: 'Briefly summarise the content of the text.'

findings.before: sich unterhalten: chat; entertain
findings.after: sich unterhalten: chat, talk; unterhalten: entertain; support (financially), maintain
findings.why: der Unterhalt is derived from this entry and its why relies on 'support, keep', but the en never gives that sense. 'entertain' is also not reflexive.

findings.before: vorhalten; zuhalten; mithalten; herhalten
findings.after: add: die Zurückhaltung (restraint), die Erhaltung (preservation), die Enthaltung (abstention), der Anhalter (hitchhiker), das Behältnis (container, formal), nachhalten (business: follow up, keep track)
findings.why: B2 tiles zurück/er/ent + -ung, an + -er, be + -nis and nach + bare verb build common real words (Zurückhaltung and Erhaltung are frequent B2 words). They must not be called wrong.

findings.before: the formal objection (against a decision)
findings.after: the objection (in court: 'Objection!'; against a fine or tax decision)
findings.why: der Widerspruch is on the same B2 board and is the standard legal term for an objection against a Bescheid (Widerspruch einlegen, Widerspruchsverfahren). The current clue fits both words.

findings.before: Ich lege gegen den Bescheid Einspruch ein.
findings.after: Ich lege gegen den Steuerbescheid Einspruch ein.
findings.why: Against most administrative Bescheide the remedy is Widerspruch. Einspruch is right for tax and fine decisions, so name one. exEn: 'I am lodging an objection to the tax assessment.'

findings.before: Main stress on dem-: DEMentsprechend.
findings.after: Often stressed on dem- (DEMentsprechend); dementsprEchend is also heard.
findings.why: Both stress patterns are standard in speech. The note should not present one as the only correct form.

findings.before: zersprechen; vorsprechen; mitsprechen; lossprechen
findings.after: add: die Versprechung (promise, often 'leere Versprechungen'), die Entsprechung (equivalent)
findings.why: The ver + -ung (A2, B1) and ent + -ung (B1) tiles build these real, common words. They must not be called wrong.

findings.before: zersprechen; vorsprechen; mitsprechen; lossprechen
findings.after: add: einsprechen (record a voice text: eine Ansage einsprechen), die Einsprache (Swiss for Einspruch), widersprechend (participle)
findings.why: The B2 tiles ein + bare verb, ein + -e and wider + ppr build real words.

findings.before: zuschreiben; nachschreiben; hinschreiben; widerschreiben
findings.after: add: die Abschreibung (depreciation; A2 and B2 boards), die Einschreibung (enrolment), die Verschreibung (prescription), die Aufschrift (label, inscription), die Mitschrift (notes, transcript) (B1 board), die Abschrift (copy), die Umschrift (transcription), die Umschreibung (paraphrase), die Überschreibung (transfer, overwriting), abschriftlich (B2 board)
findings.why: Every one of these can be built from the tiles on these boards and is a real word. Aufschrift, Abschrift and Einschreibung are common, so the game must not call them wrong.

findings.before: copy (from someone)
findings.after: copy (from someone, from a source); write off (a cost, a person)
findings.why: 'write off' (Ich habe ihn abgeschrieben; steuerlich abschreiben) is a common second sense.

findings.before: Ich schreibe mich für den Kurs ein.
findings.after: Morgen schreibe ich mich an der Uni ein.
findings.why: For an ordinary course, Germans say 'sich für einen Kurs anmelden'. sich einschreiben is typical for university enrolment, and that also matches eingeschrieben.adj. exEn: 'Tomorrow I'm enrolling at university.'

findings.before: to look up (from a book)
findings.after: to look up, raise your eyes (from a book)
findings.why: 'to look up (from a book)' reads in English as looking something up in a book, which is nachsehen (en: 'check, look up'). A learner will reasonably build nachsehen.

findings.before: Ich sehe meinen Fehler ein.
findings.after: Er sieht seinen Fehler einfach nicht ein.
findings.why: A first-person present-tense self-report sounds staged; einsehen is typically used about someone (not) admitting something, often negated.

findings.before: I accept my mistake.
findings.after: He simply won't admit his mistake.
findings.why: 'accept my mistake' is unidiomatic English; einsehen = see/admit that one is wrong. Matches the improved example.

findings.before: to provide for, to plan (a rule)
findings.after: to provide for, to plan (what a plan or law lays down)
findings.why: '(a rule)' is unclear: it is the rule/plan that does the vorsehen, not its object.

findings.before: the visibility (in fog); a point of view
findings.after: the visibility (in fog); the view (from a seat)
findings.why: 'a point of view' invites die Ansicht ('opinion', same family) and der Standpunkt; visibility is the core sense and enough.

findings.before: ersehen; besehen; hinsehen; wegsehen
findings.after: ersehen; besehen; hinsehen; wegsehen; die Durchsicht (check, inspection); durchsichtig (transparent); einsichtig (reasonable, understanding)
findings.why: B2 board tiles durch/ein + t/ig build Durchsicht, durchsichtig (very common) and einsichtig; none is listed, so the game may reject real, common words.

findings.before: Er überfährt eine rote Ampel.
findings.after: Die Katze wurde von einem Auto überfahren.
findings.why: The example shows only the secondary, officialese sense ('eine rote Ampel überfahren'); the main sense 'run over' is never shown. Also the English clue already lists 'run over' first.

findings.before: He runs a red light.
findings.after: The cat was run over by a car.
findings.why: Matches the improved example.

findings.before: zerfahren; entfahren; widerfahren; anfahren; auffahren; ausfahren
findings.after: zerfahren; entfahren; widerfahren; anfahren; auffahren; ausfahren; die Durchfahrt (passage, way through); die Überfahrt (crossing); die Weiterfahrt (onward journey); der Mitfahrer (passenger, ride-sharer); die Mitfahrt (ride); die Vorbeifahrt (driving past)
findings.why: Board tiles build these with -t/-er: durch+t, über+t, mit+er, mit+t (B2), weiter+t, vorbei+t (B1). Durchfahrt ('Durchfahrt verboten'), Überfahrt, Weiterfahrt and Mitfahrer are common and must never be rejected.

findings.before: Ich bestehe die Prüfung.
findings.after: Hoffentlich bestehe ich die Prüfung!
findings.why: A bare present-tense 'Ich bestehe die Prüfung' is not something a native says; one says 'Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden' or expresses hope.

findings.before: I pass the exam.
findings.after: I hope I pass the exam!
findings.why: Matches the corrected example; 'I pass the exam' is also unnatural English.

findings.before: pass (an exam); bestehen aus: consist of
findings.after: pass (an exam); bestehen aus: consist of; bestehen auf: insist on; exist
findings.why: 'bestehen auf' (insist on) is a high-frequency B1 sense and 'exist' (seit 1990 bestehen) explains der Bestand.

findings.before: nicht ausstehen können: cannot stand
findings.after: nicht ausstehen können: cannot stand; be outstanding (a payment, an answer)
findings.why: 'Die Antwort steht noch aus' / 'ausstehende Zahlungen' is a common second sense the learner will meet in letters.

findings.before: Ich widerstehe der Schokolade.
findings.after: Ich kann der Schokolade einfach nicht widerstehen.
findings.why: The bare present 'Ich widerstehe der Schokolade' is stilted; the natural collocation is 'nicht widerstehen können'.

findings.before: I resist the chocolate.
findings.after: I just can't resist chocolate.
findings.why: 'I resist the chocolate' is unnatural English; matches the corrected example.

findings.after: There is also a separable überstehen (hat/ist übergestanden): stick out, overhang (das Brett steht 5 cm über).
findings.why: Prevents the learner inferring that über-stehen can only be inseparable.

findings.before: erstehen; anstehen; zustehen
findings.after: erstehen; anstehen; zustehen; der Aufstand (uprising); der Ausstand (strike); beständig (constant, resistant); verständig (sensible); umständlich (cumbersome, long-winded); geständig (having confessed); abstehen (stick out); vorstehen (preside over; protrude); umstehen (surround); der Überstand (overhang)
findings.why: Board tiles build these: auf/aus+stem, be/ver+ig, ab (B1); um+lich, ge+ig, vor, um, über+stem, auf+stem (B2). Aufstand, beständig and umständlich are very common and must never be rejected.

findings.before: to decide (to do something); to pass (a law)
findings.after: to decide (often together, formally); to pass (a law)
findings.why: 'to decide (to do something)' fits sich entschließen equally ('sich entschließen, etwas zu tun'), and both are on the B1 and B2 boards. Point to the group/formal decision that is typical of beschließen.

findings.before: the degree (a finished qualification)
findings.after: the qualification (school or university); the end
findings.why: 'degree' suggests only a university degree; Abschluss is also the school-leaving qualification (Realschulabschluss) and the end of something.

findings.before: prep
findings.after: prep (+Gen), also adv
findings.why: Also adverb: 'bis einschließlich Freitag' (up to and including Friday); the id already says adv.

findings.after: der Aufschluss (information, insight: Aufschluss geben); der Einschluss (inclusion); die Erschließung (development of an area); die Entschließung (formal resolution); die Einschließung; die Ausschließung; die Abschließung
findings.why: Board tiles build these (auf/ein+stem; er/ent/ein/aus/ab+ung). Erschließung, Aufschluss and Entschließung are common and must never be rejected; the RARE list is empty.

findings.before: the purchase (buying something)
findings.after: the purchase (of a car, a flat)
findings.why: der Einkauf is also 'purchase (buying something)' and its own en lists 'purchase'; both are on the B1 board, so a learner can reasonably build Einkauf. Big one-off purchases (Kauf eines Autos, einer Wohnung) are Kauf, never Einkauf.

findings.before: verb |  (no split marker)
findings.after: verb | SPLITS
findings.why: blaumachen is separable (Er macht heute blau; hat blaugemacht); the split field is empty and only the note says it splits, so the form card teaches the wrong class.

findings.before: the payment (a transfer of money)
findings.after: a payment (one sum paid, e.g. each month)
findings.why: die Bezahlung also means 'payment' (Die Bezahlung erfolgt per Überweisung) and Einzahlung/Auszahlung are transfers of money too; all are on the B1 board. Zahlung is the countable one (eine monatliche Zahlung, mehrere Zahlungen), which the new clue points at.

findings.before: to pay out; to pay off (sich)
findings.after: to pay out (money to someone)
findings.why: abzahlen's clue is 'to pay off (in instalments)'; both verbs share the B1 and B2 boards, so 'pay off' in two clues invites the wrong answer. Keep the sich-sense in en, not in the clue.

findings.before: to state, to mean (a rule, a study)
findings.after: to say (of a rule or text: 'The rule ___ that …')
findings.why: aussagen (on the same B2 board) is also used of studies and data (Was sagt die Studie aus?) and its en contains 'state'. A sentence-frame clue makes besagen the only fit.

findings.before: Die Polizei hat das gestohlene Auto aufgefunden.
findings.after: Das gestohlene Auto wurde in einem Wald aufgefunden.
findings.why: auffinden is overwhelmingly used in the passive (wurde aufgefunden, tot aufgefunden); the active 'Die Polizei hat ... aufgefunden' sounds stilted; a native says 'hat ... gefunden' there.

findings.before: The police have located the stolen car.
findings.after: The stolen car was found in a forest.
findings.why: Matches the improved passive example.

findings.before: try, attempt; taste (food)
findings.after: try, attempt; (regional, dated) taste (food)
findings.why: 'versuchen' for tasting food is southern/Austrian or dated; standard de-DE says probieren. Unmarked, the learner will say 'Versuch mal den Kuchen' where Germans expect 'Probier mal'.

findings.before: We can no longer afford to bear these costs.
findings.after: These costs are no longer sustainable for us.
findings.why: The English is clumsy ('afford to bear'); 'nicht mehr tragbar' = no longer sustainable/acceptable.

findings.before: The annual statement brought a large extra payment to make.
findings.after: After the annual bill we had to pay a large amount extra.
findings.why: The English is unnatural; the new version says what the German means.

findings.after: The verb is mostly used as ausverkauft (sold out) and in der Ausverkauf (clearance sale); active forms like 'verkauft alles aus' are rarer.
findings.why: The active example is grammatical but much rarer than the participle; the learner should know which form is the everyday one.

findings.before: A lot has changed over time.
findings.after: She won the ten-kilometre race.
findings.why: The translation belongs to a different sentence. The example is 'Sie hat den Lauf über zehn Kilometer gewonnen.'

findings.before: The division of the city lasted almost thirty years.
findings.after: The division of Germany lasted more than forty years.
findings.why: The translation does not match the example (Deutschlands / über vierzig Jahre). It looks like it was taken from a Berlin sentence, and it teaches a wrong fact about the example.

findings.before: to hand out (tests); to deal (cards)
findings.after: to deal (cards); to dish out (criticism)
findings.why: 'Hand out (tests)' fits verteilen just as well. The verteilen example is even the same scene (Der Lehrer verteilt die Arbeitsblätter). Both prefixes are on the B2 board (aus, ver), so a learner can reasonably answer verteilen. Dealing cards and 'gut austeilen (und nicht einstecken)' belong only to austeilen.

findings.before: Der Lehrer teilt die Tests aus.
findings.after: Wer teilt die Karten aus?
findings.why: This avoids the near-duplicate of the verteilen example, which implies the two verbs are one and the same, and it matches the new clue.

findings.before: The teacher hands out the tests.
findings.after: Who's dealing (the cards)?
findings.why: Follows the new example.

findings.before: to develop (a solution) by working on it
findings.after: to gain by your own hard work (sich etwas: a good reputation); to work out (a topic, in class)
findings.why: 'Eine Lösung ausarbeiten' is just as idiomatic as 'eine Lösung erarbeiten'. With ausarbeiten (clue: work out in detail) on the same B2 board, the current clue does not single out erarbeiten. 'Sich etwas erarbeiten' (earn by work) is unique to er-.

findings.before: to listen in (on a call)
findings.after: to overhear, to listen in (on a conversation next to you)
findings.why: 'Listen in on a call' is exactly what abhören means (ein Telefongespräch abhören). abhören (clue: tap a phone line) is on the same B2 board, so a learner can reasonably build abhören. mithören is hearing along because you happen to be there.

findings.before: to contribute, to work on (a project)
findings.after: to be part of the team on (a project); to take part (in class)
findings.why: 'To work on' alone points to bearbeiten (work on a text or case), which is on the same A2/B1 boards. The mit- idea (as one of several people) should be in the clue.

findings.before: She is helping out on (collaborating on) the new project.
findings.after: She is working on the new project (as part of the team).
findings.why: The bracketed double translation is clumsy, and 'helping out' understates it. Mitarbeiten is regular participation, not occasional help.

findings.before: Thank you for working with us so well!
findings.after: Thank you for the great cooperation!
findings.why: The English is unnatural. The German is the fixed closing formula of business letters and emails, and English has its own equivalent ('Thanks for the great collaboration/cooperation').

findings.before: revision (of a text)
findings.after: revision (of a text); overwork, exhaustion (from working too much)
findings.why: The verb entry gives 'sich überarbeiten: overwork', and the noun has that sense too (an Überarbeitung leiden).

findings.before: to come to terms with (the past)
findings.after: to come to terms with (a country's past, its history)
findings.why: verarbeiten (en: come to terms with an experience) is also said of one's own past ('die Vergangenheit verarbeiten'). Collective, historical reckoning is what makes it aufarbeiten.

findings.before: Welche Staatsangehörigkeit steht in Ihrem Pass?
findings.after: Welche Staatsangehörigkeit haben Sie?
findings.why: The suggested sentence is the standard form question at A1. The current sentence is understandable but less idiomatic.

findings.before: What nationality does your passport say?
findings.after: What is your nationality?
findings.why: Follows the new example.

findings.before: Unfortunately the yoghurt is already past its date.
findings.after: Unfortunately the yoghurt is already out of date.
findings.why: 'Past its date' is not idiomatic. Natural options are 'out of date' or 'past its use-by date'.

findings.before: Der Hund ist gestern weggelaufen.
findings.after: Als Kind ist er einmal von zu Hause weggelaufen.
findings.why: The clue says 'from home'. A runaway pet is the entlaufen example (Katze ... entlaufen), so a child keeps the two apart for the learner.

findings.before: The dog ran away yesterday.
findings.after: As a child he once ran away from home.
findings.why: Follows the new example.

findings.before: to plan (your time); to divide into groups
findings.after: to plan, budget (your time, your money)
findings.why: 'In Gruppen aufteilen' is as common as 'einteilen'. aufteilen and einteilen are both on the A2 and B1 boards, so 'divide into groups' points both ways. Budgeting time or money is the einteilen-specific sense.

findings.before: The teacher does the dividing into groups.
findings.after: The teacher decides who goes in which group.
findings.why: The current English is stilted.

findings.before: We furnished the flat cosily.
findings.after: We've furnished the flat to make it really cosy.
findings.why: 'Furnished ... cosily' is unnatural English.

findings.before: Man hat sie zur Richterin am Landgericht berufen.
findings.after: Sie wurde als Professorin an die Universität Wien berufen.
findings.why: In everyday German judges are mostly 'ernannt'. The textbook collocation for berufen is a professor being called to a chair (einen Ruf erhalten / berufen werden).

findings.before: She has been appointed judge at the regional court.
findings.after: She was appointed professor at the University of Vienna.
findings.why: Follows the new example.

findings.before: She beat the old record by two seconds.
findings.after: She beat the old record by ten centimetres.
findings.why: The German says um zehn Zentimeter; the English invents 'two seconds' (and a time record would be unterboten, not überboten).

findings.before: A bare stem with a vowel change, but das: an exception to learn.
findings.after: an + ge + bot: the -ge- inside makes it das, like das Gebot, das Gebiet, das Aufgebot.
findings.why: Angebot is not a bare stem: it contains ge- (An-ge-bot). Calling it a bare stem teaches a false pattern (a learner would expect *Anbot) and hides the real reason for das (ge- collective/neuter nouns).

findings.before: das Gebiet: a bare-stem noun but das, like das Angebot.
findings.after: das Gebiet: ge- + biet; nouns built with ge- are mostly das (das Gebot, das Gebäude).
findings.why: Gebiet is ge- + stem, not a bare stem; the ge- is exactly why it is neuter.

findings.before: das Gebot: a bare-stem noun but das, like das Angebot and das Verbot. Not on a board: it is built from the same tiles as das Gebiet.
findings.after: das Gebot: ge- + bot, and ge- nouns are mostly das (like das Gebiet, das Angebot). Not on a board: it is built from the same tiles as das Gebiet.
findings.why: Gebot contains ge-; it is not a bare-stem noun.

findings.before: das Aufgebot: a bare-stem noun but das, like das Angebot.
findings.after: das Aufgebot: auf + ge + bot; the -ge- makes it das, like das Angebot.
findings.why: Auf-ge-bot contains ge-; not a bare stem.

findings.before: provider, supplier (a woman or a firm: die Firma)
findings.after: provider, supplier (a woman)
findings.why: Firms are normally called der Anbieter regardless of die Firma; 'die Firma ist Anbieterin' exists only in legalese. The note makes a learner over-apply die Anbieterin to companies.

findings.before: Sie ist Anbieterin von Sprachkursen in der Stadt.
findings.after: Als selbstständige Anbieterin von Yogakursen muss sie viel Werbung machen.
findings.why: 'Sie ist Anbieterin von Sprachkursen' is stiff officialese; a native would say 'Sie bietet Sprachkurse an'. The current exEn even translates it with the verb. exEn would become: 'As a self-employed provider of yoga classes, she has to do a lot of advertising.'

findings.before: on board B1
findings.after: B2 board only
findings.why: A feminine B2 agent noun of modest frequency adds nothing at B1; Anbieter is enough there.

findings.before: The doctor has told him not to smoke.
findings.after: The doctor has forbidden him to smoke.
findings.why: 'told him not to smoke' weakens verbieten to a piece of advice; the point of the word is forbid.

findings.before: to open (a packet); to dawn (a day)
findings.after: to start on (a new packet); to dawn (a day)
findings.why: 'to open' alone also fits aufbrechen (break open), which is on the same B2 board; 'start on' is the specific anbrechen sense.

findings.before: RARE
findings.after: not rare
findings.why: gebrechlich is an ordinary current word (alt und gebrechlich), not rare; keep it off boards for derivability, but do not label it rare.

findings.before: I asked several companies for a quote.
findings.after: I asked several companies whether they still had any appointments free.
findings.why: The German asks whether they have free appointments; nothing about a quote. Translation does not match.

findings.before: The low prices tempt many people to buy.
findings.after: The low prices tempt many people into impulse buys.
findings.why: Spontankäufe = impulse buys; the translation drops the point (being led into something unplanned).

findings.before: varying, differing (in size, opinion)
findings.after: differing from one another (the adjective of 'the difference')
findings.why: 'varying, differing' is a fair clue for verschieden too, and verschieden's clue 'various' is a fair clue for unterschiedlich; both are on board B1. As written a learner can reasonably swap them. Anchoring unterschiedlich to der Unterschied separates them.

findings.before: various (several kinds of)
findings.after: various, all sorts of (kinds of bread, of people)
findings.why: Keep verschieden on 'various/all sorts of' and move unterschiedlich to 'differing from one another'; see the unterschiedlich finding.

findings.before: ab = off: you give off your vote; or you tune things to each other.
findings.after: ab here marks completion: you cast your vote and the matter is settled; abstimmen auf = tune one thing to another.
findings.why: 'give off your vote' is not English and not a real picture of ab-.

findings.before: to join (a club, a party)
findings.after: to join, become a member (with the dative: einem Verein …)
findings.why: 'to join a party' is equally in eine Partei eintreten, and eintreten is on the same B1 board; a learner can reasonably build eintreten.

findings.before: the joining (of a club, a union)
findings.after: the accession (of a country to the EU), joining
findings.why: der Eintritt (in einen Verein) also means joining, and ein is an extra tile on the B2 board, so Eintritt is a reasonable answer. EU-Beitritt is the sense only Beitritt has.

findings.before: ist eingetreten
findings.after: ist/hat eingetreten
findings.why: eine Tür eintreten (kick in a door) takes haben and is common; en could add 'kick in (a door; hat)'.

findings.before: Die Zuweisung der Räume kommt per E-Mail.
findings.after: Die Zuweisung der Räume erfolgt per E-Mail.
findings.why: 'Die Zuweisung kommt per E-Mail' is a category mismatch (an allocation is not a message); erfolgen is the natural collocation. exEn: 'Rooms are allocated by email.'

findings.before: the instruction (how to do something)
findings.after: the instruction, order (given by the boss)
findings.why: 'how to do something' points to Anleitung (manual); Anweisung is an instruction someone gives you.
